notes.meaning: Pilate asked what crime Jesus had done, because under Roman law he found no fault in Him. Instead of naming any real wrongdoing, the angry mob simply shouted louder for Him to be executed on a cross. The governor gave in to their noise instead of defending an innocent man.

Seeing that a dangerous riot was starting, Pilate took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd to claim he was free from guilt. Hand-washing was an ancient custom used to show publicly that a person was clean from a crime. Yet washing his hands could not remove his real guilt, because as a judge he had the duty and power to protect the innocent.

The crowd boldly shouted that they and their children would accept full responsibility for Jesus' death. They took on this curse rashly, fully convinced that their cause was right. God's judgment later fell upon the city when Jerusalem was destroyed, yet in great mercy God also saved many who turned to Christ in faith.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that the Greek phrase lacks a verb and records the crowd's reckless shout at that moment rather than a divine prophecy, warning that these words must never be used to blame the Jewish people as a whole or excuse hatred toward them.

notes.meaning: Pilate released the dangerous criminal Barabbas and ordered Jesus to be whipped before being crucified. Roman flogging was a brutal beating with leather whips that tore open the flesh. Jesus took this severe suffering so that guilty sinners could be delivered from God's judgment.

The soldiers took Jesus inside the governor's palace, known as the Praetorium, and gathered hundreds of troops around Him. These rough men made the hall of justice into a stage for cruelty and sport. They assembled the entire unit to join in taunting a prisoner who had no one to defend Him.

The soldiers stripped off Jesus' outer clothes and draped an old red military cloak over Him to look like royal robes. Roman commanders and rulers wore scarlet and purple, so the troops used this faded garment to ridicule His claim to be a king. By bearing this shameful treatment, Jesus began to cover our spiritual nakedness with His righteousness.

They twisted prickly thorn branches into a mock crown and pressed it onto His head, placing a wooden reed in His right hand as a fake royal sceptre. Then they knelt before Him in mock worship, shouting, 'Hail, King of the Jews!' While they meant it as a cruel joke, the thorns recalled the curse brought into the world by sin, which Jesus willingly bore for us.

The soldiers spat on Jesus to show their utter disgust and contempt. Then they grabbed the reed staff from His hand and repeatedly struck Him on the head, pounding the sharp thorns into His scalp. The Lord endured this intense pain and humiliation without striking back or uttering a threat.

Once they grew tired of mocking Him, the soldiers stripped off the red cloak and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him away toward the execution site outside the city walls. Jesus went forward quietly like a sacrificial lamb being led to the altar to die for His people.

Along the road, the soldiers forced a traveler named Simon from Cyrene in North Africa to carry Jesus' heavy cross. Jesus had carried it at first, but He was physically exhausted from a sleepless night and brutal beatings. Simon was pressed into service against his will, reminding believers that following Christ means being ready to share His reproach.

They brought Jesus to a place called Golgotha, an Aramaic name meaning 'The Place of the Skull.' This was an execution hill outside the walls of Jerusalem where criminals were put to death. Christ suffered outside the city gates so that He might remove our curse and bring us into God's heavenly kingdom.

Before nailing Him up, they offered Jesus wine mixed with bitter gall, a common drink given to numb pain and cloud the mind of a dying criminal. Jesus tasted it to show He did not despise the offer, but He refused to drink it down. He chose to remain fully conscious so He could finish His work of atonement, which means paying the full penalty to make sinners right with God.

After fastening Him to the cross, the soldiers took His garments and divided them up by casting lots, like rolling dice. This fulfilled the ancient prophecy of Psalm 22:18, which said that enemies would divide His clothes and cast lots for His robe. Jesus was stripped bare on the cross so that believers could be clothed in His righteousness.

The soldiers sat down at the foot of the cross to keep constant guard over Jesus. Their job was to prevent any friends or sympathetic crowds from attempting a rescue before the prisoner died. Unknowingly, these hardened soldiers were placed there to become eyewitnesses to the death of the Son of God.

Above Jesus' head, the soldiers fastened a written notice of the official charge against Him: 'THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.' Pilate put this up to explain the death sentence and insult the Jewish rulers who demanded it. Yet God directed the wording so that the placard proclaimed the absolute truth: Jesus truly is the Messiah, God's promised King.

Two highway robbers were crucified on either side of Jesus, placing Him right in the center as if He were the worst criminal of them all. This fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah 53:12, which said He would be counted among lawbreakers. He was placed between outlaws so that guilty people could one day be counted among God's saints.

People walking by on the busy road hurled insults at Jesus and shook their heads in scorn. Shaking the head was a common gesture showing triumph over someone who had fallen into ruin, just as Psalm 22:7 had foretold. Even while dying in agony, Christ had to endure the heartless jeers of everyday travelers.

The crowd taunted Him about His words concerning the temple, daring Him to save Himself and step down from the cross if He was really the Son of God. They twisted His teaching about raising the temple of His body from death in three days. Their challenge repeated the very temptation Satan gave Jesus in the wilderness, urging Him to prove His power without enduring the cross.

The chief priests, teachers of the law, and Jewish elders joined the crowd in mocking Jesus. These respected leaders forgot all sense of dignity and decency to ridicule a dying man. Their open cruelty proved how blind and hardened they had become toward God's truth.

The leaders sneered that Jesus had saved others from illness and death, yet could not save Himself. They promised to believe in Him if He would only climb down from the cross right then. But Jesus stayed on the cross out of love; if He had saved Himself from death, He could not have saved anyone else.

The leaders scoffed that since Jesus trusted in God, God should rescue Him now if He really cared for Him. Without realizing it, these religious men quoted the exact words predicted of Christ's mockers in Psalm 22:8. They assumed that His suffering meant God had abandoned Him, but in truth, Jesus was pleasing His Father by paying the penalty for human sin.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Catholic and Orthodox readers note that this mock challenge closely parallels Wisdom 2:13-20, an Old Testament book in their Bibles that describes ungodly men testing a righteous sufferer who calls himself a child of God.

notes.meaning: Even the two robbers hanging beside Jesus joined in insulting Him at first. Despite their own terrible pain and approaching death, these criminals added their voices to the abuse heaped on Christ. Yet one of them later repented after seeing Jesus' patience, showing that even the most hardened sinner can find mercy.
